plain: The first reliable start of the rainy season. We look for enough rain to wet the soil, with no long dry spell straight after.
A run of days with almost no rain. A long dry spell while a crop is flowering can reduce the harvest.
A ten-day period: days 1 to 10, 11 to 20, or 21 to the end of the month. There are 36 in a year.
A satellite measure of how green and healthy plants are. Low values suggest bare soil or dry plants.
How much water is held in the soil around the roots. Satellite estimates are coarse and cannot see one field.
Ground with little or no plant cover. Bare soil is exposed to sun, wind and rain, so it can lose water and wash away.
How often a crop's rainfall, dry-spell and heat limits were all met in the past seasons we counted.
Changing the crop grown on a field from one season to the next, instead of growing the same crop every year.
Some plants, such as legumes, take nitrogen from the air and add it to the soil. The next crop can use it.
A plant that carries its seeds in pods, such as cowpea or groundnut. Most legumes add nitrogen to the soil.
A grass grown for grain, such as maize, sorghum or millet. Cereals usually need more soil nitrogen.
A what-if run with less rain or more heat. It shows how the ranking reacts. It is not a forecast.
How much trust to place in a location's numbers. It is higher when two independent satellite rainfall records agree.
A local agricultural adviser who knows your area, your soil and the varieties that work nearby.
